title: Structure and Properties of Multicomponent Arc-PVD Ti–Cr–Mo–Ni–N Coatings on Carbide Alloys HG20, HS123, HV420 and Tool Steel C80W1
content: The arc-PVD Ti–Cr–Mo–Ni–N coatings on HG20, HS123, HV420 carbide alloys and C80W1 tool steel, while having approximately the same elemental and phase compositions, differ in morphology, macrostructure, and level of macrostresses. When deposited on steel, the coating exhibits macrolayering, a more extended coating–substrate transition zone, and develops tensile macrostresses, in contrast to the coatings on carbide alloys, which develop compressive macrostresses. The behaviour can be explained by the overheating of the coating during deposition, which results from ion bombardment and is more pronounced on steel due to its poorer thermal diffusivity relative to carbide alloys. The CLTE difference between steel and the coating is significantly larger than that between the carbides and the coating, further contributing to the effect. It was found that, considering these features, the Ti–Cr–Mo–Ni–N coating on steel exhibits lower hardness (~20.3GPa), lower adhesion strength to the substrate (Lc3≈30N, the indenter load at scratch testing corresponding to the onset of coating wear), and a higher wear intensity at room temperature and 500°C (49.80 and 74.20·10−6 mm3·N−1·m−1, respectively), as compared with the hardness values of 25.1–21.7GPa, Lc3≈100N, and wear intensity (corresponding to the absence of a visible wear crater) for the Ti–Cr–Mo–Ni–N coatings on the aforementioned carbide alloys.
